title: Why Are Whale Strandings Still a Mystery?
summary: Hosts open with tour announcements (Toronto, Chicago, Vancouver, Minneapolis, Austin, Lawrence KS, Brooklyn, Atlanta charity show) and then examine mass whale strandings: the February 2017 pilot whale stranding at Farewell Spit, New Zealand, and the causes debated (social bonds, illness, sonar and navy exercises, chronic noise, shallow water and echolocation). They discuss the Project Jonah guidelines, the dilemma of euthanizing stranded whales, a drug cocktail protocol (medazolam, azaperone, potassium chloride) delivered by industrial needles near the fins, the SWEED sperm whale euthanasia device, exsanguination, and the 1970 Florence, Oregon exploding sperm whale. A listener mail segment asks for help identifying a podcast about a crazy doctor, and the episode closes with sign-off.

segments.title: Tour announcements
segments.summary: Hosts announce live tour dates and cities, ticket sales date, and a charity benefit show in Atlanta, directing listeners to the tour website.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode with light banter about the show's T-shirt slogans and the word mystery.

segments.title: Farewell Spit pilot whale stranding
segments.summary: Hosts describe the February 2017 stranding of about 600 pilot whales at Farewell Spit in Golden Bay, New Zealand, and the response by locals and Project Jonah. They note New Zealand's high rate of whale strandings and that mass strandings happen in coastal countries generally.

segments.title: Why whales are stranded and what suffering they face
segments.summary: Hosts describe the suffering of stranded whales, including skin burns, gull attacks, and suffocation under their own weight. They note that the reasons for strandings remain uncertain and that the research record reaches back centuries.

segments.title: Causes of mass strandings
segments.summary: Hosts cover species that most often strand, such as short-finned pilot whales, false killer whales, melon-headed whales, Cuvier's beaked whales and sperm whales. They discuss hypotheses including sickness or injury, following prey into shallow water, echolocation failure in shallows, and disorientation, with North Sea whales found to have digested oceanic squid.

segments.title: Social bonds and stranding response
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the social caring hypothesis, where pod members stay with a stranded member. They mention the post-2016 workshop on strandings, the proposed International Strandings Network, and the Entanglement Network.

segments.title: Sonar, Navy exercises and decompression sickness
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the link between military sonar and whale strandings, including the Greece NATO exercise with twelve Cuvier's beaked whales, the Bahamas 2000 event with inner ear hemorrhaging, and Canary Islands beaked whales showing signs of decompression sickness. They cover a 2017 Journal of Experimental Biology study by Terry Williams and the Navy agreement to halt certain exercises near Hawaii and southern California. They also mention chronic shipping noise.

segments.title: Dolphins staying with an injured companion
segments.summary: Hosts recount a researcher's account of two short-beaked common dolphins at the Tife Estuary in West Wales, where a sick dolphin was accompanied by an uninjured companion that stayed close and whistled.

segments.title: Whether to refloat or euthanize stranded whales
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how to care for stranded cetaceans, the danger of approaching a beached whale, the difficulty of spotting internal injuries, and the prevailing scientific view that stranded whales, especially large ones, are often best euthanized.

segments.title: Humane euthanasia methods for whales
segments.summary: Hosts discuss euthanasia options: phenobarbital, which persists in tissue and poisoned a dog that ate whale meat; a drug cocktail of medazolam, azaperone, and potassium chloride given in sequence and delivered by industrial needles near the fins; the SWEED anti-tank gun for sperm whales; and exsanguination.

segments.title: 1970 Florence, Oregon exploding whale
segments.summary: Hosts recount the November 1970 incident in Florence, Oregon, where a dead 45-foot sperm whale was blown up with dynamite by the state highway division with Navy advice. Blubber rained down on onlookers and a car was crushed. They also discuss whale falls, disposal rules, and the danger of decomposition gas.

segments.title: New Zealand travel aside
segments.summary: Hosts briefly discuss New Zealand as a place to visit and its friendly, safe atmosphere.

segments.title: Listener mail: crazy doctor podcast
segments.summary: A listener asks for help identifying a podcast episode about a doctor who was run out of multiple towns. The hosts do not recall it. They also read a note from Olivia Barrett and mention the show's Birmingham performance and social handles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off with contact information and the website.
